slides.say: A cylinder or a cone is different. The volume changes by what they changed, the radius or the height, and by how much.

slides: Remember from the solids lesson. If only the height changes, and the radius stays, the volume changes in the same way.

slides.say: Think of a soda can. Put another can on top of it. The height is twice as much, and so is the volume.
Put a third can on top. Three times the height, three times the volume.
So height times five gives volume times five, as long as the radius stays the same.
Our problem is when they change the radius. When the radius changes, the volume changes by the square of the change.
Radius times two gives volume times two squared, four. Radius times three gives volume times three squared, nine.
Why? Here it's hard to see, because the old cylinder sits inside the wider one. So let's see it in the formula.
The volume of a cylinder is pi r squared, times h.
The new radius is two r. So the new volume is pi, times the square of two r, times h.
at: The new radius is two r

slides.say: Inside the brackets, each part gets squared. Two squared is four, and r squared stays. So it's four pi r squared h.

slides: And pi r squared h is the old volume. So the volume is four times as big. The four came from the two, squared.
Careful with the brackets. If we square only the r, we lose the four.

slides.say: A cone works the same way. Its volume is the cylinder's volume, divided by three.
Let's make its height five times bigger. The new volume is pi r squared, times five h, divided by three.
We take the five out, and we get five times the old volume. The divided by three is in both volumes, so it doesn't change the factor.

slides: So for a cone too, height times five gives volume times five. And radius times two gives volume times four. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next part.
